detail:
The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) describes several research directions for Chiari malformations (CM). One line of work is genetic: because changes in genes can cause many brain malformations, NINDS scientists are looking for gene changes that could act through the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway, which is essential for normal brain development, and related pathways, research the institute says may lead to new diagnostic tests and better treatment options. Other investigators study how growth factors are expressed during development of the brain, skull, spine, and spinal cord.

NINDS also describes natural-history research on syringomyelia, the fluid-filled cyst in the spinal cord associated with CM: scientists are recording more than five years of symptoms, muscle strength, general function, and MRI findings in people receiving standard treatment, to learn what influences its development, progression, and relief. Related work includes MRI-based biomarkers to help doctors decide on surgery, improved imaging for earlier diagnosis, and Common Data Elements that standardize how CM research describes symptoms, imaging findings, and outcomes. An NIH-funded study of surgery for Chiari I with syringomyelia in children found that adding duraplasty to bone removal led to fewer symptoms and a smaller syrinx at one year, with higher early complication rates that were comparable by six months.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about Chiari malformation research and clinical trials.
sourceName: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
summary: NINDS describes Chiari malformation research directions including genetic studies of the PI3K-AKT pathway, a five-year natural-history study of syringomyelia, MRI biomarkers, and standardized Common Data Elements for trials.
takeaways: genetic studies focus on pathways essential to brain development
a long-term study tracks syringomyelia symptoms, strength, and MRI findings
research participation is optional; talk to your doctor about studies
title: Chiari Malformation: research into genes, imaging, and syringomyelia
